posts.caption:
When your calendar has no room for anything to go wrong, eventually everything might go wrong.

🏁 Subscribe to get weekly newsletters: link in bio!

We all have that voice of doom that tells us we’re not good enough, the idea won’t work, or we should just stop. 

Harlan Coben talks about learning to push past that voice and keep creating. ✍️🎧 

Tune into this week's episode wherever you get your podcasts 👊

“It’s my therapy,” says Debbie. 

At 69, she is still jumping at least once a month. 

It hasn’t been easy - and I jump with people who are in their 20’s who progress much faster than I do. But I keep pushing forward with my goals in mind. 

I can’t count the number of times I’ve told myself I should just quit. One of those times, I wrote down the benefits of skydiving for me. 

These are the positives that have come out of my skydiving experience, but it can apply to any sport. It’s not easy. It takes commitment and work. 

But the benefits are enormous:

I have to work out regularly & eat healthy to be able to do this.
I’m learning something new at this stage in life.
It’s a technical & physical challenge in freefall and canopy.
I’m constantly problem solving “on the fly”
I’m always striving to be better.
I feel better mentally & emotionally 
It gives me a great sense of accomplishment.
It has helped with my coordination & reflexes.
It keeps my brain and my body active.
It calms me.
I can be an inspiration to other women who think their lives are “over”

#itsnevertoolate and #wearenevertooold 

If this story inspired you please share 🙏💟

“If you can’t find time to write, then writing isn’t a priority.”

Harlan Coben doesn’t mince words when it comes to making time for the work. ✍️ We all get 24 hours a day. The question is what we choose to make room for.

🎧 Listen wherever you get your podcasts, or watch on my YouTube channel 👍

Read my latest newsletter to learn how to tell whether something belongs in your life or back in the drawer ☑️

When AI sounds confident, how do we know when it’s wrong?

🎙️ Hear the full conversation with Jimmy Wales on Remarkable People.

Standing still while everything around you moves is its own kind of falling behind.

Wikipedia can get things wrong, but humans can spot and correct mistakes. With AI, a plausible but wrong answer can slip through, and there’s often no way to fix it. 

Don’t miss Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales on Remarkable People. Watch on Guy’s YouTube or listen wherever you get your podcasts. 🎙️
@kaisallas took us on his boat to surf at Threes!

Ritual can be an antidote to loneliness, polarization, and what Bruce Feiler calls “decivilization.” 🤝 

Shared experiences give us a reason to gather, listen, and find meaning together. In a world pulling us apart, ritual can bring us back to one another. 🌎
Got my Fall/Winter COVID vaccine today.

In a moment of rare humility, I told David Whyte I am a poetry Luddite and asked for the equivalent of Poetry For Dummies. He told me no such book exists—and I would have to get over the “dummy ditch” myself.

David is a poet, philosopher, and performer whose books Consolations and Consolations II take familiar words and turn them over until you see them differently.

Here’s what stuck with me:

Anger is the deepest form of care. It can be care that has no articulation yet—boiling over because we cannot say what is happening in our broken heart.

The words we avoid may carry the most weight. Regret. Despair. Vanity. Death. He even wrote an essay on “the.”
Regret isn’t the enemy. He sees it as an admission that we are fallible—and a way of paying attention to the future.

Stop waiting for perfect conditions. Whyte once needed a quiet study to write. Then he wrote “Regret” on gold-edged paper in a French restaurant and realized he could write anywhere. Starbucks, the Tube, his phone—it all works.

Listen before you read. Poetry is a spoken art, so hear great poets and actors read it, attend live readings, and then try saying it yourself.

My favorite moment? I told him there was a reason he is David Whyte and I am Guy Kawasaki, because he writes in Granada and I write in Starbucks. His response: “Oh no, I write in Starbucks too.”

Watch or listen to the full conversation at RemarkablePeople.com, my Youtube channel, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Are you a poetry Luddite too?

—Guy

#RemarkablePeople #DavidWhyte #Consolations #Poetry Writing

The words you avoid are the ones you need.’

Inherit. Excavate. Subvert.

There is no Poetry For Dummies.

Get over yourself. Then write.

What moves us always comes from what is hidden.

analysis.summary: Guy blends a high‑profile tech‑evangelist career with a public‑spokesperson role as author, podcaster and educator. He lives by the principle of helping others become remarkable, constantly creating content about creativity, AI, rituals and personal growth. His Instagram shows a mix of thought‑leadership posts, occasional personal adventures (boat trips, sky‑diving), and a focus on health routines and lifelong learning.
